Article Title: From today, households across Great Britain can plug solar panels into a standard socket; 800W kits could supply up to 20% of home electricity use and save £110 a year
Article Text:
Making solar easier for renters and flats

Strict safety rules for plug-in systems

Growing demand for home solar

Households across Great Britain can now generate their own solar power using a standard three-pin wall socket, under new rules designed to cut energy bills and make clean electricity more accessible. The legal change, which came into force on 27 August 2026, allows people in England, Scotland and Wales to buy portable solar panel kits rated up to 800 watts and plug them directly into their home electricity supply without hiring an electrician. According to estimates from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, the devices can provide up to 20 per cent of an average home's electricity use and save households up to £110 a year.The change comes as energy prices in Britain face fresh pressure. Energy regulator Ofgem has announced a 4 per cent rise in the domestic energy price cap from October, mainly because of higher wholesale fuel costs linked to continuing geopolitical tensions around Iran. Under the new rules, changes to the Plugs and Sockets etc. (Safety) Regulations 1994 and the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations 2002 through Statutory Instrument 2026/848 mean households no longer need specialist wiring or professional installation for small solar systems.Major retailers including Amazon, Currys, Argos and Wickes have announced plans to sell approved kits online and in their stores. "From this summer, we are giving more families the ability to power their homes with clean homegrown energy," said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK Energy Secretary, describing the technology as a simple and affordable way for households to manage their energy bills.Until now, home solar in Great Britain was mostly an option for property owners who could afford to spend thousands of pounds on permanent rooftop systems. The new plug-in technology is aimed particularly at renters, flat owners and people living in smaller terraced homes who may not be able to install traditional solar panels. The systems can use up to two solar panels connected to an 800-watt micro-inverter. The inverter changes the direct current produced by the panels into alternating current that can be used through a normal household electricity circuit. The electricity is used inside the home and first offsets power being consumed by appliances that are always running, such as fridges, Wi-Fi routers, televisions and devices on standby. Green energy groups welcomed the change, calling it an important step towards wider access to small-scale renewable power."This will bring cheap, clean power to households that have not been able to access the benefits of solar and batteries," said Chris Hewett, Chief Executive Officer of trade association Solar Energy UK. Trevor Hutchings, Chief Executive Officer of the Renewable Energy Association, described the move as a major step towards making renewable energy available to more people. "Our electricity prices are some of the highest because of our exposure to volatile international gas markets. Innovations like plug-in solar and the wider renewables roll out will help us bring down bills and strengthen our energy sovereignty," Hutchings said.The approval of plug-in solar systems follows safety testing of micro-inverters and household wiring. Government officials said British technical requirements are stricter than those used in some parts of continental Europe, where more than 500,000 balcony solar systems were connected in Germany during 2025. All approved British kits must have automatic anti-islanding protection. The system cuts power from the plug within 100 milliseconds if the device is unplugged or the local electricity supply fails. This prevents the exposed plug from remaining live and creating a risk of electric shock. The rules also place limits on how the systems can be used. Each household can have only one plug-in solar device. It must be connected directly to a fixed wall socket and cannot be used with an extension lead, multi-way adaptor or cable reel. Battery storage systems are not included in the new rules and cannot currently be connected through the plug-in route. Fire safety rules also restrict where the panels can be installed. They cannot be mounted on timber balconies, high-pressure laminate cladding or external walls that are undergoing safety work. Mounting systems must be non-permanent and reversible, while tenants and other residents need written permission from their landlord or freeholder before fixing panels to external structures.The new rules come as residential solar installations continue to grow across Great Britain. Data from the Microgeneration Certification Scheme recorded almost 150,000 certified rooftop solar installations in the first six months of 2026. That was 17 per cent higher than the previous record for the same period in 2025. Government estimates show that traditional rooftop solar can save homeowners up to £480 a year. However, officials expect plug-in systems to attract many more households because they are cheaper and easier to install. Similar systems typically cost between £400 and £600 in European markets. After installing a system, owners must enter its details on the official UK Plug-In Solar Registration portal. This will help local electricity network operators track the amount of small-scale generation connected to the grid. The new rules currently apply across England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is expected to consider similar measures under its own energy policies.
Article Summary: Home solar can provide up to 20 per cent of an average home's electricity use and save households up to £110 a year. The new plug-in technology is aimed particularly at renters, flat owners and people living in smaller terraced homes. Amazon, Currys, Argos and Wickes have announced plans to sell approved kits online.

Article Title: Hegseth asked top US military general to drop Kid Rock helicopter probe before firing him: Report
Article Text:
US War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Gen. Randy George, the US Army chief of staff who was forced to retire earlier this year, was reportedly asked to drop an investigation into a low-flying helicopter incident near musician Kid Rock’s Tennessee home days before his removal.Gen. Chris LaNeve, who was then the Army’s No. 2 officer and is now serving as acting Army chief of staff, told George that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted the probe to be discontinued, The Washington Post reported, citing people familiar with the discussions.George, however, told colleagues that he believed the Army should complete the investigation in accordance with protocol. He was reportedly unnerved by the interaction with LaNeve, according to the report, which cited two other sources.The development offers a new detail about the circumstances surrounding George’s abrupt departure from the Army.Hegseth asked him to retire effective April 2, without publicly giving a reason for the decision.The controversy stems from a March 28 incident in which two Army AH-64 Apache helicopters flew at low altitude near Kid Rock’s property in Tennessee. The Army initially suspended the pilots and launched an administrative investigation to determine whether any rules had been violated.Hegseth subsequently reversed the decision, lifting the suspensions and saying there would be “no punishment” and “no investigation”.Kid Rock, whose legal name is Robert Ritchie, had posted videos of the helicopters flying near his home and later praised the pilots.Weeks after the incident, Hegseth and Kid Rock were also seen flying together in Apache helicopters from Fort Belvoir in Virginia.LaNeve, meanwhile, has been serving as acting Army chief of staff since George’s departure and is expected to be formally nominated for the post.His potential nomination has faced opposition from Republican Sen Joni Ernst of Iowa, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.Hegseth has defended LaNeve, calling him “precisely the kind of leader the US Army needs right now” and saying he is not interested in “playing politics in Washington”.George had been expected to remain Army chief of staff until 2027, completing the usual four-year term. His removal, along with the departure or impending departure of other senior Army officials, has raised concerns about a leadership vacuum at the service.
Article Summary: Gen. Randy George was forced to retire earlier this year. He was reportedly asked to drop an investigation into a low-flying helicopter incident near musician Kid Rock’s Tennessee home days before his removal. The controversy stems from a March 28 incident in which two Army AH-64 Apache helicopters flew at low altitude near Kid Rock's property in Tennessee.

Article Title: In 1904, a 1,227-foot Cincinnati railroad warehouse was among the world’s longest buildings; 122 years later, 210 feet were removed for a new bridge and its old bricks are being reused
Article Text:
Historic photo of the completed B&O freight warehouse, now Longworth Hall

The building had shrunk before

Old bricks will help rebuild the east end

The new bridge behind changes

Longworth Hall, a historic railroad freight warehouse in Cincinnati, is now shorter than it was for most of its history. About 210 feet of the world’s longest buildings has been removed to make way for a new bridge over the Ohio River.The demolition is part of the Brent Spence companion bridge project. According to NPR, work on the new bridge officially began with a groundbreaking ceremony in May, and the removal of part of Longworth Hall has been one of the first visible changes linked to the project.The historic building at 700 W Pete Rose Way was completed in 1904 by the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad as a warehouse for rail freight. At the time, it was 1,227 feet long and was described as one of the longest buildings in the world.Most of Longworth Hall will remain standing, however. The section being removed is largely an addition constructed in the 1960s. According to the Cincinnati Enquirer, contractors took about six months to remove roughly one-fifth of the building. A time-lapse video also shows the demolition taking place in less than a minute.The latest demolition is not the first time Longworth Hall has lost part of its length. In 1961, about 150 feet of the building was removed to make room for Interstate 75 on the Cincinnati side of the Ohio River.That section was later restored.Ironically, the part being removed now was itself added in the 1960s, after the building had already been shortened for the interstate.Longworth Hall has also changed ownership over the decades. In 1985, it was sold to Roy and Ron Schweitzer and Rudy Hermes, with the Schweitzers taking ownership soon afterwards. The building was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.In 2023, the Ohio Department of Transportation acquired the property. ODOT now owns the building and plans to put it up for sale after the new bridge is completed.The current work is being carried out carefully because the remaining structure is historic. While much of the 210-foot section is being demolished, a portion of the original building will be taken apart in a way that allows its old bricks to be saved.The next stage will involve rebuilding Longworth Hall's east end with bricks recovered during the demolition. The work will also include cleaning the exterior, replacing deteriorating bricks and mortar, and improving the building's exterior windows.Other original materials left over from the demolition will also be saved for future maintenance and repairs.Ohio Department of Transportation Press Secretary Matt Bruning says, "The idea is that once all of this work is done, you will drive by on I-75 and look over at Longworth Hall and it will look like it did in 1904 when it was finished. Only it will be shorter," Bruning said.ODOT said the rebuilding of the east-facing wall is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. Demolition of the 1960s addition was expected to be completed within a couple of months, it was reported in March.Longworth Hall will also undergo extensive masonry work and upgrades to its historic windows before ODOT eventually transfers the property to its next owner.The changes to Longworth Hall are directly linked to the long-planned Brent Spence companion bridge. The new bridge is being built immediately west of the existing Brent Spence Bridge and will provide a new crossing over the Ohio River.The project is expected to cost almost $4.4 billion. That figure is higher than the $3.6 billion estimate given the previous year, before the final bridge design was selected.The bridge project will bring more visible construction activity around the area. Bruning said the work would eventually move into the river and towards the approaches to the bridge.
Article Summary: Longworth Hall, a historic railroad freight warehouse in Cincinnati, is now shorter than it was for most of its history. About 210 feet of the world’s longest buildings has been removed to make way for a new bridge over the Ohio River. The section being removed is largely an addition constructed in the 1960s.

Article Title: RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat's US event organiser AHEAD’s X account suspended ahead of programme
Article Text:
​RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s event organiser’s X account has been suspended two days before the Madison Square Garden programme.

The X (formerly Twitter) account of the organisation hosting Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat 's event at New York's Madison Square Garden has been suspended days before the event.The American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) was listed as “unavailable” on X under the handle @AheadForum1. The account was suspended ahead of Bhagwat's scheduled address at the Universal Oneness Celebration at the Infosys Theatre at Madison Square Garden on August 29.The programme is expected to draw around 5,000 Indian Americans as part of the RSS's global outreach during its centenary year. The organisation later issued a statement saying, "AHEAD believes the suspension may have occurred in error."Earlier this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he did not support the planned event, while acknowledging that his office may not have the authority to cancel a private gathering.“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani told reporters on Tuesday.Mamdani's comments have triggered criticism among sections of the Indian-American diaspora and have also drawn opposing reactions from Indian political parties.His remarks came as left-liberal groups criticised the event and called for its cancellation.The controversy has also prompted a security advisory from the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), a US-based non-profit organisation. HAF urged people attending the event to remain vigilant, stay aware of their surroundings and keep interactions civil.HAF said the advisory followed attempts by activists targeting Hindu Americans to disrupt and cancel the celebration.It also called on Mamdani to ensure the safety of people attending the event.The event has also drawn scrutiny from the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), which has urged the US government to consider sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials it alleges are involved in religious freedom violations in India.“We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat and making him ineligible for future entry into the United States,” the body said.The commission is chaired by Pakistani-American Asif Mahmood.India's Ministry of External Affairs has previously rejected USCIRF's assessments, accusing the body of bias and questioning its credibility. During an August 21 press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the commission had made what he described as “incorrect and provocative statements about India” for years.“We all know this is a biased institution. For years, it has made incorrect and provocative statements about India. We should ignore such institutions, as they have their own agendas and lack credibility,” Jaiswal said.
Article Summary: The X (formerly Twitter) account of the organisation hosting Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat's event at New York's Madison Square Garden has been suspended. The programme is expected to draw around 5,000 Indian Americans as part of the RSS's global outreach during its centenary year. The organisation later issued a statement saying, "AHEAD believes the suspension may have occurred in error"

Article Title: Meet Daniel Janzen: The ecologist who turned 169,000 hectares of Costa Rica into a giant forest filled with biodiversity
Article Text:
Image(s): Left/Wikipedia/Right/Impact Destinations/GDFCF

How Daniel Janzen became fascinated by tropical ecosystems and field biology

Why Costa Rica became central to Daniel Janzen’s conservation work

Winnie Hallwachs and Dan Janzen (Image: By Shayla White)

From cataloguing species to building a long-term biodiversity legacy

Daniel H. Janzen is a biologist whose career has blurred the traditional boundaries between field ecology, evolutionary science and conservation. For decades, his work has centred on tropical ecosystems, particularly the forests of Costa Rica, where he studied the intricate relationships between plants, insects and other organisms. His research eventually developed into something much larger than documenting species. Alongside biologist Winnie Hallwachs, Janzen helped shape the Área de Conservación Guanacaste (ACG), a vast conservation landscape in north-western Costa Rica that connects forests, volcanic ecosystems and marine environments. His work has also explored how conservation can function alongside local communities rather than treating protected areas as places completely separated from society. The University of Pennsylvania identifies Janzen as a leading figure in conservation biology, while his research has produced hundreds of scientific publications and influenced modern approaches to tropical biodiversity. His career demonstrates how understanding an ecosystem can become the first step towards protecting it for generations.Janzen's relationship with tropical biology began when he was young.According to the University of Pennsylvania and a biographical account published by the National Academy of Sciences, his interest in the tropics developed during a butterfly-collecting trip to Mexico when he was 14. He later studied biology at the University of Minnesota before earning his PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. His research became particularly focused on the relationships between tropical plants and animals. Insects, especially caterpillars and their interactions with host plants and parasites, became an important part of his scientific work. Since the late 1970s, Janzen and Hallwachs have carried out extensive field observations in Costa Rica's Área de Conservación Guanacaste. Their long-term work has helped document the complexity of tropical ecosystems rather than treating species as isolated components.Janzen's role changed significantly during the 1980s, when scientific research began evolving into a much broader conservation effort. After being asked to examine environmental damage in Costa Rica, he became increasingly concerned that simply creating protected areas would not necessarily guarantee their survival. His focus shifted towards finding ways for conservation areas to function as part of the surrounding society. This philosophy became closely associated with the Área de Conservación Guanacaste. Janzen and Hallwachs helped develop the landscape into a large-scale conservation experiment involving restoration, biodiversity research, local employment and partnerships. A 2020 paper by Janzen and Hallwachs describes the ACG as a government-NGO conservation entity spanning roughly 169,000 hectares and incorporating ecosystems extending from the Pacific Ocean through dry forests and volcanic landscapes towards wetter forests. The approach challenged the idea that successful conservation simply means keeping people outside protected areas. Instead, Janzen argued for integrating biodiversity protection with the communities and institutions surrounding it.One of Janzen's most influential contributions has been his emphasis on understanding biodiversity at an enormous scale. The ACG has become both a conservation landscape and a long-term scientific research site, where species can be documented while their relationships with ecosystems are studied over decades. Janzen's work has also contributed to the development of DNA barcoding as a tool for identifying species. The University of Costa Rica notes that he helped promote the use of genetic “barcodes” to recognise species through molecular techniques, while his broader scientific output includes more than 500 publications. The scale of the ACG reflects the ambition behind this approach. Janzen and Hallwachs have described the area as a long-term effort to restore and conserve a connected tropical landscape while integrating it into Costa Rican society. For Janzen, therefore, conservation is not simply about preserving a snapshot of nature. It is about understanding how an ecosystem works, documenting its biological wealth and creating the social and scientific structures needed to keep that diversity alive far into the future.
Article Summary: Daniel Janzen is a biologist whose career has blurred the traditional boundaries between field ecology, evolutionary science and conservation. For decades, his work has centred on tropical ecosystems, particularly the forests of Costa Rica. Alongside biologist Winnie Hallwachs, Janzen helped shape the Área de Conservación Guanacaste (ACG), a vast conservation landscape. The ACG has become a conservation landscape and a long-term scientific research site.

Article Title: US citizenship applicants face renewed neighbourhood scrutiny under new USCIS guidance
Article Text:
US citizenship applicants may face scrutiny from neighbours, co-workers and others under new USCIS guidelines

Those applying for US citizenship could face scrutiny from their neighbours, co-workers and wider communities as the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has formally laid out how it will conduct neighbourhood investigations during the naturalisation (citizenship) process.The new guidance, issued on Aug 25, took effect immediately and applies to citizenship applications pending on that date as well as those filed thereafter. Investigators may seek information from people who know the applicant, including neighbours, landlords, employers, co-workers, business associates, customers and others. The scope can be wide, covering an applicant's family and marital history, social activities and associations, employment and business activities, financial obligations and reputation in the community.The inquiry may also examine criminal history, international travel and foreign activities, as well as current and previous residences. USCIS may assess an applicant's credibility and truthfulness, loyalty to the US and respect for the principles in the US Constitution.As was reported earlier by TOI, USCIS had resumed such investigations in Aug 2025, after the practice had largely been abandoned in 1991. The latest guidance explains how the investigations may be used to corroborate information supplied by applicants and gather information that may not emerge from documents or the naturalisation interview.However, it should be noted that the investigations will not automatically apply to every applicant. USCIS said its ‘Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate’, in coordination with field operations, will decide whether an investigation should be conducted or waived based on an individualised and discretionary assessment of the case.USCIS added that information from members of the community can assist in determining whether an applicant meets citizenship requirements, including good moral character and being well disposed to the good order and happiness of the US.Applicants can voluntarily submit character-reference or testimonial letters with their Form N-400 application. USCIS says such letters, preferably from US citizens who are not family members, may be considered when deciding whether to waive a neighbourhood investigation. However, immigration attorneys point out that even if these letters are submitted, USCIS officials may still decide to speak to neighbours, co-workers, employers and others.For the Indian diaspora, which has navigated lengthy green card waits before becoming eligible for naturalisation, the prospect of a review extending beyond their application papers and citizenship interview could add a layer of uncertainty. Immigration attorneys believe that, by and large, a history of stable employment, regular tax payments and participation in their children's school activities or the wider community could stand Indian applicants in good stead. However, the bottom line is that it remains to be seen how this new guidance will be enforced.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has formally laid out how it will conduct neighbourhood investigations during the naturalisation (citizenship) process. Investigators may seek information from people who know the applicant, including neighbours, landlords, employers, co-workers, business associates, customers and others. USCIS may assess an applicant's credibility and truthfulness, loyalty to the US and respect for the principles in the US Constitution.

Article Title: 'It's your sense of entitlement': US officials slam Indian-origin entrepreneur Ankit Gupta over H-1B comments
Article Text:
Indian-origin serial entrepreneur Ankit Gupta, general partner of YC, is at the center of a major social media storm over his comments on H-1B which he deleted later.

Who is Ankit Gupta ? What is the latest H-1B controversy?

Ankit Gupta was accused of deriding Americans as he was defending the H-1B immigrant culture.

White House official reacts, YC CEO issues statement

Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest, following which Gupta made his X account private. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement". Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.Gupta, a distinguished computer scientist from Harvard, is a serial entrepreneur and currently a partner of Y Combinator. Before joining YC, he was the co-founder and CTO of Reveries Labs. The controversy that he landed in stemmed from his comment on JD Vance's post."If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans," Vice President JD Vance wrote on X, reacting to the Donald Trump administration's new H-1B visa fee. "in a win for the woke left DEI is back," Ankit Gupta commented, suggesting that if Americans have to be hired because they are Americans and not because of their skill, then it is DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inlcusion) only.The now-deleted post and the sarcasm did not go down well with America First commentators, and then it came to the notice of the DOL's Inspector General."Ankit Gupta thinks hiring Americans first—in America—is “DEI.” No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first. American companies. American jobs. American workers first. If that offends you, the problem isn’t America. It’s your sense of entitlement," D'Esposito said.As Gupta defended the H-1B hiring by Silicon Valley, he asked one commentator: 'what elements of H-1B immigrant culture do you not like? is it the willingness to work long hours? Or perhaps the education focus of their children?""Leaving trash everywhere, scamming people, endemic pathological dishonesty, atrocious aesthetic taste, need I go on," the commentator replied. "It's giving flyover country," Gupta wrote. Social media users started flagging this comment as a racist attack aimed at rural white Americans and asked YC to take action against Gupta."Hey @ycombinator this is a racist attack aimed at rural White Americans. Your policies mention that you do not tolerate any racism. It states that racial discrimination is a fireable offense. When can we expect you to fire Ankit Gupta?" one wrote.Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson, responded to the controversy and called YCombinator "a front for the far left"."Y Combinator is a supposed champion of “Little Tech” but perhaps they’re nothing more than a front for the far left. I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind," Ferguson wrote, referring to Gupta."The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world," he said.Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan issued a statement saying that YC supports hiring and funding Americans.
Article Summary: Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement" Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.

Article Title: Hindu priest arrested in Canada for sexually assaulting woman under guise of healing
Article Text:
Rajendranauth Doodnauth MARAJ,/Image: Durham Regional Police

A US-based Hindu priest has been arrested in Oshawa, Canada, for sexually assaulting a woman under the guise of a religious healing ceremony.Police said the victim and her family had hired the priest, identified as Rajendranauth Doodnauth Maraj, 50, to travel from the US to perform a Hindu religious ceremony. Maraj is from Richmond Hill, New York.According to Durham Regional Police, Maraj told the woman that she was possessed by evil spirits and convinced her that she needed a specific ceremony to be healed. Police said he then exploited her trust in his religious role and brought her to a private location, where he allegedly sexually assaulted her while claiming to be carrying out the ceremony.Officers from the East Division responded to a sexual assault call on Tuesday, August 25, in the area of Harmony Road North and Conlin Road East. Maraj was later taken into custody .He has been charged with one count of sexual assault and was held for a bail hearing.
Article Summary: Rajendranauth Doodnauth Maraj, 50, is from Richmond Hill, New York. He told the woman that she was possessed by evil spirits and convinced her that she needed a specific ceremony to be healed. Police said he exploited her trust in his religious role and brought her to a private location.

Article Title: US college student shot dead by police after knocking on wrong house amid burglary call
Article Text:
22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania. (AP Photo)

A 22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania after he mistakenly went to the wrong house and was waiting for his friends to pick him up, his father said.Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in, CNN reported citing Montgomery County district attorney’s office. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead.Pysher’s father, Glen Pysher, said his son had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.According to what his son’s friends told him, Pysher took a wrong turn through the woods and mistakenly went to a house he believed belonged to a friend.Pysher was carrying only his phone and a backpack with clothes and a few beers, his father said. He allegedly tried to open the door and called out, “Hey! Open the door!” believing he was at his friend’s home.After realising the mistake, Pysher sat on the back porch and contacted his friends.They then started heading to the house to pick him up.His friends later saw police and emergency vehicles at the location and initially believed Pysher would be arrested for public drunkenness. Instead, he had been shot.Pysher’s father said his son was on a FaceTime call with his friends at 12:32 am, while police were dispatched at 12:30 am and arrived at 12:34 am, according to a Montgomery County Department of Public Safety dispatch record.The father questioned what happened during the brief interval before his son was shot.Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Chief Al Werner has declined to release details, including the names of the officers involved, pending the investigation.The Montgomery County Detective Bureau is investigating the shooting, the district attorney’s office said.Pysher was due to begin his senior year at Saint Elizabeth University in New Jersey, where he planned to play baseball. He hoped to become a high school history teacher and coach after graduating.His father described him as kind-hearted and loving, saying former teammates, coaches and others had reached out with memories of him since his death.The family has also said it has received little information from police.Pysher’s father said he was recently told he could collect his son’s favourite black shoes so they could be used for his burial, but was later told officials needed to consider whether they could release them.
Article Summary: Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead. He had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.

Article Title: A Michigan businessman brought nine white-tailed deer to North Manitou Island in 1926; decades later, the artificial herd had grown to an estimated 2,000
Article Text:
PC: The Leelanau Historical Society

How William R. Angell brought nine white-tailed deer to North Manitou Island

PC: The Leelanau Historical Society

How deer became the main attraction for wealthy sportsmen

How nine deer grew to 700 on North Manitou Island

Why North Manitou Island became a private hunting retreat

North Manitou Island was never home to large game until a wealthy Michigan businessman decided it should be. In the mid-1920s, William R. Angell, the driving force behind the Manitou Island Association, set out to turn the 15,000-acre island into a private hunting and fishing retreat for himself and his associates. His answer was to bring white-tailed deer to a landscape that had never supported them, nine animals shipped over from the mainland with no natural predators waiting on the other side. What began as a modest experiment in stocking a sportsman's playground would, within a few decades, grow into one of the largest deer herds ever recorded on an island of its size, reaching an estimated 2,000 by the early 1980s and forcing a reckoning between private ambition and the land's own limits. That story starts with Angell himself, and the choices he made in 1926.In the mid-1920s, businessman William R. Angell set in motion one of the most consequential wildlife experiments in the history of North Manitou Island. Angell, the principal owner behind the Manitou Island Association, wanted to turn the 15,000-acre island into an exclusive retreat where he and his associates could hunt and fish away from the mainland crowds.White-tailed deer were central to that ambition, and in 1926 he had a small founding herd brought over to establish the population from scratch.As per The Leelanau Historical Society, a slightly fuller account of the same event, recording that the white-tailed fawns were sourced from the Munising State Forest and arrived nine strong, eight does and a single buck, chosen in the hope that their bloodline would eventually produce impressive racks for hunters to pursue. Whichever figure is taken as the precise starting point, both accounts agree that the white-tailed deer were an entirely artificial addition to an island that had never supported large game before.Angell's motive for introducing deer was never purely sentimental. He and his fellow landowners in the Manitou Island Association were building a business, and a stocked hunting ground was the product they wished to sell. Raccoons had already been released in 1924 for the same purpose, but it was the deer that would come to define the island's reputation among wealthy sportsmen throughout the following decades.The early years were not without difficulty. Farm dogs on the island reportedly killed three of the original fawns when they tried to herd the newcomers as though they were cattle, mistaking their unfamiliar behaviour for something that needed correcting. Once that initial disruption passed, however, the surviving deer found ideal conditions on North Manitou. With no natural predators and abundant vegetation to browse, the small founding group began to multiply at a pace that would soon outstrip the island's capacity to support them.Unchecked breeding transformed Angell's modest founding stock into a genuine management problem within little more than a decade. By 1937, the population had swollen to an estimated 700 animals, prompting the Manitou Island Association to organise the island's first official deer hunt with assistance from the State of Michigan, alongside a winter supplemental feeding programme to keep the herd alive through the harsher months. By the 1950s that figure had climbed to around 1,000, and naturalists and state officials returned periodically over the following decades to count the herd and assess its condition.The growth did not stop there. According to the National Park Service, "By counts in the early 1980s, there were about 2,000 deer on the island," a scale that had visibly reshaped the landscape itself. The deer stripped the island of almost every plant they found palatable, leaving a distinctive browse line five to six feet above the ground and allowing unpalatable species such as American beech to flourish unchecked in their place, a stark contrast to the lush understorey still found on neighbouring South Manitou Island.For much of the twentieth century, the herd Angell had founded served a narrow and well-heeled clientele. Hunters were generally guests of the island's principal owners or corporate clients drawn from firms such as Continental Motors and Shakespeare Rod and Reel, along with government contractors and, during the 1950s and 1960s, associates of the Detroit mafia. Each guest was guaranteed a deer, driven out to a guide-selected spot in the morning and returned to the lodge for lunch before an evening of cards and conversation. Guides ensured a steady supply for the table by shooting animals from moving vehicles when demand outpaced what visiting hunters managed to bag themselves.That arrangement could not survive the island's transfer into public ownership. Negotiations between the Manitou Island Association and the US Justice Department over incorporating the island into the Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore began in 1977 and dragged on for seven contentious years, and when the Association withdrew its staff in the autumn of 1978, the supplemental feeding programme that had sustained Angell's herd through the winters came to an abrupt end. Hundreds of deer and turkeys starved over the two winters that followed, a grim coda to a herd that had begun, half a century earlier, as a handful of fawns brought ashore for the pleasure of a wealthy few.
Article Summary: William R. Angell brought nine white-tailed deer to North Manitou Island in 1926. He wanted to turn the 15,000-acre island into a private hunting and fishing retreat for himself and his associates. By 1937, the population had swollen to an estimated 700 animals. By the 1950s that figure had climbed to around 1,000.

Article Title: Researchers examined pilot whales stranded around Hawaii over 13 years; 3 had swallowed up to 12 pounds of marine debris, including as many as 35,543 pieces of plastic in a single stomach
Article Text:
Pilot whales stranded around Hawaii

Fishing waste is the biggest threat

Deep-sea hunting increases the risk

Plastic can cause long-term harm

Years of research

Massive tangles of discarded fishing lines, ropes and plastic bags are harming marine life in the Pacific, with deep-diving whales swallowing thousands of plastic pieces in Hawaiian waters. A 13-year study of stranded short-finned pilot whales around the main Hawaiian Islands found that nearly 23 per cent of the animals examined had swallowed synthetic waste. Researchers at the Health and Stranding Lab at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that three adult males had each swallowed up to 12 pounds (5.4 kilograms) of ocean debris. The findings, published in the scientific journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, offer detailed evidence of how plastic pollution is entering the digestive systems of deep-sea predators. Full necropsies of the three whales revealed huge amounts of synthetic waste packed inside their stomachs. Tests showed that the whales had swallowed between 6,283 and 35,543 separate pieces of plastic larger than 5 millimetres, about the width of a standard pencil eraser.“The presence of human-made materials in the stomachs of these ocean sentinels serves as a stark reminder of the impact of global plastic pollution,” said Kristi West, director of the UH Health and Stranding Lab and corresponding author on the study.“It is a clear message of the importance of keeping these materials out of our ocean.”Most of the waste found inside the whales came from abandoned, lost or discarded fishing gear, often known as ghost gear. Strong monofilament fishing lines, synthetic ropes and pieces of fishing nets made up most of the material recovered from the animals. The second-largest group was flexible plastic sheets, including carrier bags, household rubbish sacks and industrial packaging. Although small pieces were much more common, larger objects accounted for most of the total weight. Items longer than 200 millimetres, or about 8 inches, made up more than 70 per cent of the total weight of the plastic recovered from the three whales.Short-finned pilot whales (Globicephala macrorhynchus) are large marine mammals found in tropical and warm temperate oceans around the world. They are capable of deep dives and can travel hundreds of metres below the surface while hunting prey with echolocation. Researchers said the whales may be especially vulnerable to plastic because of their diet. Pilot whales mainly eat squid, which can move and feel similar to floating plastic sheets, submerged bags and fishing lines drifting through the water. The location of the Hawaiian Islands may also increase the danger. The islands are downwind and downstream from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a large area of floating marine waste northeast of Hawaii. Ocean currents can carry fishing gear and other plastic waste towards Hawaiian waters, where pilot whales feed.Despite carrying large amounts of plastic, all three adult males were in normal physical condition before they stranded. Researchers did not identify the debris as the main or immediate cause of death. However, scientists warned that this does not mean the whales were unharmed. Large amounts of plastic can take up valuable space in the stomach, leaving less room for food and potentially causing long-term nutritional stress. Over time, this could weaken the immune system of marine mammals. Plastic can also create chemical risks. Synthetic materials in the ocean can absorb pollutants, including polychlorinated biphenyls and heavy metals, and can release chemicals from the plastic itself. As plastic breaks down inside an animal, some of these substances can enter surrounding tissues and build up in organs and blubber, potentially affecting health and reproduction.The study's findings came from more than seven years of field collection, laboratory work and tissue preparation. A team of 25 researchers, graduate students and field technicians helped recover the stranded whales, carry out necropsies and sort thousands of pieces of plastic. The project received financial support from the Environmental Readiness Division of the Commander, United States Pacific Fleet, as well as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries John H. Prescott Marine Mammal Rescue Assistance Grant programme. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi said stranded whales can provide important information about the health of remote marine ecosystems that are otherwise difficult to study. The large amounts of plastic found in Hawaiian pilot whales underline the need for stronger international action on discarded fishing gear and single-use plastics before pollution causes further damage to marine food webs.
Article Summary: 13-year study of stranded short-finned pilot whales around the main Hawaiian Islands found that nearly 23 per cent of the animals examined had swallowed synthetic waste. Tests showed that the whales had swallowed between 6,283 and 35,543 separate pieces of plastic larger than 5 millimetres.

Article Title: In the 1950s, a Chinese American Army veteran turned a New York mountain into a ski resort; in 2026, its 440 acres were bought for $3.3 million to join a state park
Article Text:
Mt Cathalia rises above downtown Ellenvill (Picture: Chonogram magazine)

The place's Chinese American history

The 440-acre property sits between the North and South Gully areas of Minnewaska. (Open state institute photo)

Connecting protected areas

Ski runs become meadows

In the 1950s, Chinese American Army veteran Joseph Tso bought a 440-acre mountain property in Ellenville, New York, renamed it Mt Cathalia and developed a hotel and ski resort there. The property is now set to become part of Minnewaska State Park Preserve. According to Open Space Institute, the property was bought for $3.3 million and will connect two previously separated sections of the park.Mt Cathalia, also known as Mt Meenagha is the largest remaining undeveloped, privately owned parcel adjoining Minnewaska. According to Chonogram Magazine, OSI bought it from Morgan Barrington Financial Services and plans to transfer the land to New York State for inclusion in the park’s Sam’s Point Area.The property lies between Minnewaska’s North and South Gully areas, near the Ellenville Ice Caves and its addition will connect sections of protected land that were previously unlinked. The preserve would also grow to more than 24,000 acres once the transfer is completed.The mountain’s history is one reason the acquisition has drawn attention beyond its conservation value. In the 1950s, Joseph Tso, a Chinese American attorney, businessman and US Army veteran, purchased the property and renamed it Mt.Cathalia, meaning 'a little bit of China'.Tso then established a hotel and ski area on the mountain. According to OSI, Mt. Cathalia became the country’s only Chinese American-owned and operated ski resort and hotel.The resort welcomed Chinese Americans and other minority visitors who were excluded from many resorts during that period.According to Tso’s children, Cecilia and Stan Tso, the property continues to have deep meaning for their family. “Mt. Cathalia means so much to our family. We are hoping that OSI’s efforts will fulfil our parents’ dream of sharing Mt. Cathalia with everyone,” they said.The 440-acre property sits between the North and South Gully areas of Minnewaska. Its acquisition will create a link between the two sections near the Ellenville Ice Caves.Erik Kulleseid, president and CEO of OSI, says, “Mt Cathalia is an extraordinary landscape on every level- environmentally, recreationally, and historically”. He describes the purchase as another step towards creating “a corridor of permanently conserved and connected land along the entire Shawangunk Ridge.”OSI has been involved in conservation work in the Shawangunks since 1974. The organisation says it has protected more than 40,000 acres in the region and helped add 14,000 acres to Minnewaska, more than doubling the park’s size.Its work has also included restoring nearly 18 miles of Minnewaska’s historic carriage roads and raising $3 million for the Lake Minnewaska Visitor Center, which opened in 2020.The property's former ski runs have now become meadows surrounded by mature chestnut oak and pine forests. Mt Cathalia contains Shawangunk conglomerate outcrops and gullies lined with hemlock trees. OSI estimates that nearly the entire property has above-average habitat resilience. It says the mountain’s different elevations and microclimates could provide wildlife refuge as the climate changes.The land is also part of the Sandburg Creek watershed. North Gully serves as an emergency drinking-water source for Ellenville, while water from both North and South Gully eventually flows towards the Hudson River.According to OSI’s analysis, the property’s forests and soils store an estimated 132,000 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.Ellenville Mayor Evan Trent says the acquisition protects an important part of the village’s viewshed as well as one of the largest tracts in its watershed. He also hopes the mountain will eventually become a public recreational space.For now, Mt. Cathalia remains closed to visitors. The immediate plan is to complete the transfer and prepare the property for its future as part of Minnewaska State Park Preserve.
Article Summary: The 440-acre property sits between the North and South Gully areas of Minnewaska. In the 1950s, Joseph Tso, a Chinese American attorney, businessman and US Army veteran, purchased the property and renamed it Mt Cathalia, meaning 'a little bit of China' Tso then established a hotel and ski area on the mountain. According to OSI, Mt. Cathalia became the country's only Chinese American-owned and operated ski resort.

Article Title: ‘Worst 24 hours of my life’: Indo-American doctor appeals for help after parents go missing in Nepal floods
Article Text:
Ramesh Sharma, 65, and Neelam Sharma, 64/Image: X

An Indo-American doctor has made an urgent appeal for information about her parents after the couple went missing during catastrophic flash floods and landslides near the Nepal-China border while travelling on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.Radhika Sharma said her parents, Ramesh Sharma, 65, and Neelam Sharma, 64, have been “missing and unaccounted” for since they crossed the Nepal-China border at around 8am local time on Wednesday, about 40 minutes before the floods struck. She said she has not heard from them since.“It’s been probably over 24 hours, and probably been the worst 24 hours of my life, my brother’s life,” Sharma told NBC. “We’re just waiting to hear from them, and just any information, honestly.”Sharma turned to social media for help and appealed to anyone with contacts in Nepal and Tibet who might have information about her parents. In a post on X, she asked people with direct contacts in Gyirong and Tibet, local hospitals, rescue operations, government authorities or local media to contact her immediately.“I would greatly appreciate any help. Any contacts, any information,” she wrote.The couple were travelling as part of a pilgrimage to sacred Mount Kailash when the floods and landslides struck the Himalayan border region.Their disappearance comes as authorities continue searching for hundreds of people who remain unaccounted for following the disaster.The floods have killed at least 165 people in Nepal, according to figures provided by Nepalese authorities. Three deaths have also been reported in Tibet, where 558 people are missing.The figures have continued to change as authorities work to establish the full scale of the disaster. A later update put the death toll in Nepal at 270, while 826 are still missing. Nepalese officials said dozens of bridges had been destroyed and nearly 40 kilometres (25 miles) of roads damaged, making it harder for rescue teams to reach affected areas.The Nepalese Army has been using helicopters to reach people stranded by the floods. Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said more than 100 people had been rescued from flood-hit areas on Thursday morning, while at least eight foreign nationals were airlifted to Kathmandu. Army teams also evacuated people trapped inside facilities connected to the Trishuli hydropower project.The disaster has also affected Indian pilgrims travelling to Mount Kailash. An official spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said 21 Indian nationals from Tamil Nadu who had travelled for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra had been rescued in Nepal.
Article Summary: Radhika Sharma said her parents, Ramesh Sharma, 65, and Neelam Sharma, 64, have been ‘missing and unaccounted’ for since they crossed the Nepal-China border on Wednesday. The couple were travelling as part of a pilgrimage to sacred Mount Kailash.

Article Title: Massachusetts police officer resigns hours before termination hearing after allegedly using Flock and police databases to track former partner; town removed its last Flock camera
Article Text:
Representative image

A police officer in the small Massachusetts town of Stow has resigned just hours before a scheduled termination hearing, after an internal investigation found he repeatedly misused surveillance tools to track a former partner. Officer Jason Rogers allegedly used Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader system and state police databases to obtain information about the woman with no legitimate law enforcement purpose, according to town officials and police statements. In response, Stow cancelled its contract with Flock Safety and removed the town’s last Flock camera in early August, according to NBC Boston's report and official statements from the Stow Police Department. Here's what actually happened:Allegations surface after victim files complaintStow police said they first learned of the allegations on June 18, when the victim filed a formal complaint with the department. Officials did not initially disclose the exact nature of Rogers’ relationship with the victim, but local reporting and court documents indicate she was a former romantic partner.Within hours of receiving the complaint, the department placed Rogers on paid administrative leave and revoked his access to all internal systems. The swift action reflected the seriousness of the allegations: misuse of law enforcement databases is not only a policy violation, but a potential crime.What the internal investigation foundOver the next four weeks, the Stow Police Department conducted an internal affairs investigation into Rogers’ use of department resources. Investigators concluded that he had: Illegally accessed Criminal Offender Record Information (CORI) through the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) system on at least five separate occasions; and used the Flock Safety automated license plate reader system and CJIS to run vehicle information on multiple dates, without any legitimate law enforcement reason.The department said its findings sustained multiple charges against Rogers, including conduct unbecoming an officer, improper use of an official position, failure to comply with written orders, use of false and unsubstantiated search reasons, and violations of department policies governing law enforcement databases.From administrative leave to criminal chargesInitially, the Stow Select Board scheduled an employment status hearing for Rogers on July 30 to determine his future with the department. That hearing was postponed, and the town placed Rogers on unpaid administrative leave the following day. A new hearing was set for August 26.After receiving the internal affairs report, Stow police opened a separate criminal investigation. As a result, they filed a criminal complaint seeking charges against Rogers for alleged illegal use of the CORI system. The case has been forwarded to the Middlesex District Attorney’s Office for prosecution.In addition, the internal affairs report was sent to the Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST) Commission. The POST Commission has the authority to decertify officers, which would bar Rogers from working as a police officer anywhere in the state.Resignation before hearingHours before the August 26 termination hearing, Rogers resigned from the Stow Police Department, according to town officials. His resignation ends the employment proceedings but does not affect the criminal case or the POST Commission’s review of his certification.Town ends relationship with Flock SafetyIn a significant policy move, Stow police said they have terminated their relationship with Flock Safety as a direct result of Rogers’ actions. In early August, the department removed the last Flock automated license plate reader camera it operated in town.Flock Safety’s system uses high-resolution cameras and artificial intelligence to read license plates and cross-reference them with databases, helping police track stolen vehicles, locate suspects and find missing persons. But the technology also creates a detailed record of where vehicles travel, raising concerns when it is misused for personal reasons.Stow Police Chief Michael Sallese said the department will present an updated policy for automated license plate readers to the Select Board at a later date, aiming to strengthen oversight and prevent similar abuses in the future.“A serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime”In a public statement, Chief Sallese emphasised the gravity of the situation. “Law enforcement officers are entrusted with access to sensitive information solely so they can perform their official duties and protect the public...Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime,” he said.Sallese added that the department acted quickly to remove Rogers from duty and protect its systems once the complaint was received. “We conducted a thorough investigation and are pursuing both employment and criminal accountability,” he said.Town Administrator Denise Dembkoski echoed that message, stressing that Rogers’ alleged conduct does not reflect the values of the department as a whole, according to NBC Boston. “The actions of one individual do not represent the values or conduct we expect from the good and dedicated members of the Stow Police Department,” she said, as per the report.Dembkoski praised the department’s leadership for responding “immediately” and following the evidence to produce a comprehensive internal affairs report. “We will continue working to ensure that the public has confidence in how sensitive law enforcement information is accessed and protected,” she added.Part of a broader pattern in MassachusettsThe Stow case emerged just days after a similar scandal in New Bedford, where police paused their use of Flock Safety cameras after an officer was accused of using the system to track a former girlfriend’s vehicle. That case, first reported by the New Bedford Light, has prompted calls for stricter oversight of automated license plate readers across the state.More than 100 communities in Massachusetts currently use Flock technology, according to local reporting. As these tools become more widespread, the potential for misuse, especially in cases involving domestic violence, stalking or personal disputes, has become a growing concern for privacy advocates and lawmakers.Flock responds with new safeguardsIn response to mounting scrutiny, Flock Safety’s CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, announced that the company is updating its privacy and security standards. Among the changes is a mandate that all customers adopt a feature that flags abnormal activity in audit logs, which track every search and query made in the system.“We knew that abuse was a risk nine years ago, which is why we mandated that every customer had to have an audit log,” Langley said in a video statement. “We are finding bad cops and holding them accountable.”The company says it is working to improve detection of potential misuse and to support agencies in enforcing strict use policies.What comes next for Stow and its residentsFor the victim in the Stow case, the outcome of the criminal and certification proceedings will be closely watched, according to the report. She has said she changed her identity after leaving an abusive relationship, only to discover that Rogers had allegedly used police tools to track her movements.For the town, the focus now shifts to rebuilding public trust and ensuring that powerful surveillance technologies are used only for legitimate law enforcement purposes, with robust oversight and accountability. As Stow drafts its updated automated license plate reader policy, the Rogers case is likely to serve as a cautionary example of what can happen when those safeguards fail.
Article Summary: Officer Jason Rogers allegedly used Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader system and state police databases to obtain information about the woman with no legitimate law enforcement purpose. The Stow Police Department conducted an internal affairs investigation into Rogers’ use of department resources. Investigators concluded that he had: Illegally accessed Criminal Offender Record Information (CORI) through the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) system on at least five separate occasions. The case has been forwarded to the Middlesex District Attorney's Office for prosecution.

Article Title: Louisiana announces $20,000 reward after bald eagle is fatally shot near Lake Peigneur, investigators seek person responsible for killing protected bird
Article Text:
Image: Canva

Why has the bald eagle killing triggered a $20,000 reward?

Louisiana Bald Eagle (Image: Canva)

How was the Louisiana bald eagle killed?

What laws protect bald eagles in the US?

How can people report information about the Louisiana eagle killing?

The reward for information leading to a conviction in the fatal shooting of a bald eagle in southern Louisiana has risen to $20,000, as state and federal wildlife investigators continue searching for whoever killed the protected bird. The eagle was discovered injured on December 5, 2025, near the intersection of Robert Road and Wilmer Road in rural Vermilion Parish, close to Lake Peigneur. Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) agents located and captured the bird before it could be examined, but officials determined that its injuries were consistent with a fatal gunshot wound. The eagle died shortly after being found and was later sent to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for a detailed necropsy. The case has remained unresolved despite investigators receiving several tips. The Centre for Biological Diversity, which increased its contribution to the reward, is now urging anyone with information to come forward.The reward has grown substantially as investigators attempt to generate fresh leads and identify the person responsible for killing the bald eagle in Vermilion Parish, Louisiana.According to the Centre for Biological Diversity’s August 24 press release, the organisation increased its contribution to the overall reward, bringing the total to as much as $20,000 for information that leads to a conviction. The fund now includes $13,000 from the Centre for Biological Diversity, $3,500 from Humane World for Animals, $2,500 from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and up to $1,000 from Louisiana Operation Game Thief. The Center’s latest contribution follows an earlier increase in February, when it helped raise the reward to $15,000. With the case still unresolved and investigators continuing to seek information, the larger financial incentive is intended to encourage witnesses or anyone with relevant knowledge to come forward. The Centre for Biological Diversity said the increased reward could help provide the crucial lead needed to bring the case to a conclusion.The investigation began after LDWF agents were alerted to an injured bald eagle in Vermilion Parish on December 5, 2025. Personnel found the bird near Robert Road and Wilmer Road, captured it and transported it for examination. Officials determined that the eagle had suffered a fatal injury consistent with a gunshot wound, and it died soon after discovery. The remains were subsequently sent to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for a more extensive necropsy. Months later, investigators have yet to identify a suspect publicly. The LDWF and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have continued working on the case and have received numerous tips. Still, authorities are seeking additional information that could help establish who was responsible for the shooting.The shooting is being investigated as a federal wildlife offence because bald eagles are protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act. According to wildlife officials, illegally killing a bald eagle can result in a fine of up to $5,000 and as much as one year in prison, while a civil restitution fine of up to another $5,000 may also apply. The species has particular significance in the United States because the bald eagle has served as the country’s national symbol since Congress adopted it in 1782. The bird also represents one of the country's major wildlife conservation successes. After populations declined because of habitat loss, hunting and the widespread use of DDT, conservation measures helped the species recover, eventually leading to its removal from the federal endangered species list in 2007.Wildlife officials are asking anyone who may have information about the shooting to contact Louisiana Operation Game Thief. Tips can be submitted through the hotline at 1-800-442-2511 or through the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries’ tip411 programme. People can text LADWF followed by their tip to 847411, while information can also be submitted through the free LADWF Tips mobile application. The hotline and tip411 system are monitored around the clock, and authorities say people providing information can request anonymity. Investigators are particularly interested in additional information that could help establish what happened to the eagle and identify the person responsible. The Centre for Biological Diversity, which announced the increased reward on August 24, said it hopes the larger incentive will encourage someone with relevant knowledge to come forward.
Article Summary: The eagle was discovered injured on December 5, 2025, near the intersection of Robert Road and Wilmer Road in rural Vermilion Parish, close to Lake Peigneur. Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries agents located and captured the bird before it could be examined. Officials determined that its injuries were consistent with a fatal gunshot wound. The eagle died shortly after being found and was later sent to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for a detailed necropsy.

Article Title: Meet Lennox French, the North Carolina student who designed a virtual-reality classroom idea; the state approved it and he will now become the first student to build a unit for SparkNC's statewide pla
Article Text:
French’s journey started in the Spark Lab at Lexington Senior High School, where students are encouraged to explore emerging technologies and to build ideas that have real-world applications.

From a student project to an idea for the whole state

Project approved by state review

The student becomes the designer

The classroom reimagined

From Lexington to North Carolin...

A high school student's vision of a virtual classroom is about to go far beyond the walls where it started. Lennox French, a student at Lexington Senior High School in North Carolina, has been chosen to develop and implement a virtual-reality learning unit that could soon be available to students across the state. The project is a first for SparkNC, making French the first student in the program’s history to create a unit for its statewide platform, states the school website report.French’s journey started in the Spark Lab at Lexington Senior High School, where students are encouraged to explore emerging technologies and to build ideas that have real-world applications. French created a first version of a virtual-reality Spark Lab last year. His project investigated how immersive digital environments could offer new avenues for students to learn, collaborate and explore. Now the concept is in a position to reach a much larger audience, rather than being confined to a school-based experiment. French will put together a unit called Creating Digital Spaces in VR, which will take his original idea and create a structured learning event for Spark Scholars across North Carolina.The proposed course had to be reviewed by the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction before the unit could continue. The department has determined Creating Digital Spaces in VR conforms to the state’s computer science standards. Therefore, the unit satisfies SparkNC’s alignment requirements for aggregation to course credit. That approval is a big step in turning French’s student project into an educational tool with statewide importance. For Garland Beamer, a Spark Lab leader at Lexington Senior High School, the decision is also a landmark step for the school and its student innovation program.What’s interesting about French’s project is he’s not just learning to use virtual reality. He is helping to design the educational experience. In the coming months, French and Beamer will work with NCDPI, SparkNC, industry stakeholders and technology companies to flesh the concept into an engaging and practical unit. That collaboration will include refining the content, technology and learning experience so students outside of Lexington can use the platform effectively. SparkNC Executive Vise President and Co-Founder Joe Ableidinger also acknowledged the work behind the project and expressed support for the development process.The use of virtual reality as an educational tool has been researched for a long time, allowing students to engage with simulated environments rather than simply viewing information on a screen. French’s project takes that idea a step further by putting a student at the center of the design process. The aim is not just to use VR technology, but to teach students how digital spaces can be built and used for learning. This may allow Spark Scholars to develop technical and creative problem-solving skills as they learn about an emerging area of technology.The project also highlights the opportunities for students to play with technologies that are still revolutionizing education and industry. An idea born in a Spark Lab in a high school is now being scaled for students across an entire state. It shows how innovation driven by students can help expand educational opportunities for Lexington Senior High School. For French, the next few months will be spent developing an idea into an operational learning unit. His project started with the idea of a classroom in virtual reality. Now that classroom could be a shared educational experience for students well beyond his own school.Images Courtesy: istock and Lexington Senior High School
Article Summary: Lennox French, a student at Lexington Senior High School in North Carolina, has been chosen to develop and implement a virtual-reality learning unit that could soon be available to students across the state. The project is a first for SparkNC, making French the first student in the program’s history to create a unit for its statewide platform.

Article Title: Wyoming pizza shop gets fake $300 order for 18 pizzas, owner donates entire batch to hospital as former employee volunteers to deliver them to emergency room
Article Text:
$300 pizza order turned into a prank

The restaurant was already handling a busy evening

Why the restaurant did not ask for payment upfront

Owner decides to donate all 18 pizzas

Former employee volunteers to deliver the pizzas

The pizzas found a new purpose at the hospital

The owner chose a positive response to the prank

A pizza restaurant in Cheyenne, Wyoming, was left with 18 freshly made pizzas worth about $300 after a large order turned out to be fraudulent. L’Osteria Mondello had prepared the pizzas after receiving a call from someone who reportedly said they were ordering food for a children’s wrestling club. The customer never arrived to collect the order, and when restaurant owner Dave Agovic called the number provided, the person who answered said they had not placed the order. Instead of throwing away the food or simply absorbing the loss, Agovic decided to donate the pizzas to the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center. An unexpected helping hand then arrived when former restaurant employee Ryan Lemley volunteered to deliver the unwanted pizzas to hospital staff.The incident happened on August 14, 2026, when L’Osteria Mondello received an unusually large order for 18 pizzas. The caller reportedly told the restaurant that the food was intended for a children’s wrestling club, giving the staff a reason to believe it was a legitimate group order. The kitchen prepared the entire order, with the pizzas taking around 40 minutes to make. Once they were finished, the restaurant kept them warm above the ovens while waiting for the customer to arrive and collect them.Nobody showed up, however, and the situation became suspicious. Agovic eventually called the telephone number supplied with the order, only for the person who answered to say they had not ordered the pizzas. That convinced the restaurant that someone had used the number to place a fraudulent order.The fake order arrived during an especially hectic period for the restaurant. Agovic said the kitchen was simultaneously preparing another order for around 12 or 13 pizzas and a separate order for another seven or eight. That meant staff were dealing with more than 40 pizzas at roughly the same time. The restaurant became so busy that it temporarily stopped taking additional orders and warned customers that new orders could take between 1½ and 2 hours. The unexpected 18-pizza order therefore consumed significant kitchen time and ingredients at a moment when staff were already under pressure. Once the supposed customer failed to appear, the restaurant was left with a large amount of food that had been prepared specifically for an order that did not exist.Agovic said L’Osteria Mondello generally does not require customers to pay for orders in advance. His approach is based partly on trust, and he told Cowboy State Daily that a similar incident had happened only once before during his roughly 3½ years running the restaurant. The policy meant the restaurant had little protection against someone placing a large order without intending to collect it. The incident therefore cost the business not only the value of the pizzas but also the staff time and ingredients required to prepare them. Rather than immediately changing the restaurant’s approach, Agovic focused on finding a useful destination for the food that had already been made.With the order abandoned, Agovic discussed the situation with his employees and suggested taking the pizzas to a hospital instead of allowing them to go to waste. The restaurant chose the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center, turning what had started as a frustrating loss into an unexpected donation. The decision meant that the pizzas could still be eaten rather than discarded after the restaurant had spent time and money preparing them. The incident also gave the restaurant an opportunity to help people working in a demanding environment. Importantly, reports indicate that the pizzas were donated to emergency-room staff rather than specifically to patients, so the episode is best described as a donation to hospital workers.The hospital donation became possible with help from a former member of the restaurant team. Ryan Lemley, an 18-year-old who had worked at L’Osteria Mondello for more than two years, happened to stop by the restaurant while staff were deciding what to do with the pizzas. After hearing about the abandoned order, Lemley volunteered to take the food to the hospital. He delivered the pizzas to the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center, ensuring that the restaurant did not have to throw away the entire order. Agovic later praised Lemley for stepping in and described him as his “hero that day”. His involvement added an unexpected second act of kindness to an incident that had initially been caused by someone else's prank.The 18 pizzas ultimately ended up with workers at the Cheyenne Regional Medical Center emergency room. What had been prepared for a supposed children's wrestling club instead became an unplanned meal for hospital staff. The episode illustrates how quickly the value of unwanted food can change when a business finds a practical way to redirect it. Rather than allowing the food to become waste, L’Osteria Mondello used an existing community connection to put the pizzas to use. The restaurant also shared the story publicly, helping the unusual incident spread beyond Cheyenne and attracting attention because of the positive response to the prank.The incident could have ended simply as a $300 loss for a small restaurant, but Agovic's decision changed the outcome. The restaurant still absorbed the cost of the ingredients and labour, while the person who placed the order remained unidentified in the available reporting. Yet the business chose not to let the prank determine what happened to the food. By donating the 18 pizzas and accepting help from a former employee, L’Osteria Mondello turned an attempted waste of food into a gesture towards hospital workers. The episode ultimately left the restaurant out of pocket, but it also created a story about trust, community and making the best of an unexpectedly bad situation.
Article Summary: L’Osteria Mondello in Cheyenne, Wyoming, received an order for 18 pizzas. The caller told the restaurant that the food was intended for a children’s wrestling club. The customer never arrived to collect the order, and when restaurant owner Dave Agovic called the number provided, the person who answered said they had not placed the order. Instead of throwing away the food or simply absorbing the loss, Agovic decided to donate the pizzas to the hospital.

Article Title: Yellowstone visitors once used Handkerchief Pool like a natural washing machine; after a log stopped its activity in 1926, a 1929 cleanup removed 1.5 bushels of debris, including 100-plus hairpins and
Article Text:
Handkerchief Pool was a visitor favourite for its ability to pull in handkerchiefs and return them washed and clean. (NPS photos)
